tldr: Reinforcement learning enabled a humanoid robot to sit on a caster chair and move in all directions by kicking the floor. Trained without human motion data or chair state tracking, the policy transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1 robot, letting it glide smoothly while remaining seated.
hero_caption: Real-world experiment with a Unitree G1 translating and turning in all directions by kicking the floor while seated on a caster stool. The pelvis is not fixed to the chair, and the robot stably maintains its seated posture without using contact sensors.
overview:
Most humanoid locomotion research assumes a standing posture. However, robots driven by quasi-direct-drive (QDD) motors must constantly generate torque just to support their own weight while standing still. This wastes power and produces significant heat. Humans rest on office chairs during desk work, scooting around by kicking the floor with their feet. If humanoid robots could also use chairs, they could save energy and expand their workspace.

To explore this, the authors studied omnidirectional seated locomotion on a passive mobile chair without any straps or fasteners. The robot and chair move together through intermittent foot-floor propulsion. Unlike skateboards or roller skates, this task presents unique challenges: the pelvis-seat contact is unfixed, propulsion comes from direct foot contact with the floor, and motion must remain smooth in all directions.

The authors addressed this by extending a standard standing reinforcement learning environment. They added a passive chair model, seated-state rewards, and contact refinements like detailed pelvis collision meshes and elliptic friction cones. No motion imitation data was used. In addition, they conducted a $2^3 = 8$ full-factorial study across four training seeds to evaluate symmetry regularization (SY), foot-slip regularization (FS), and a command curriculum (CC).

In testing, policies completed nearly 100% of 20-second random velocity rollouts, matching or outperforming standing policies in tracking accuracy. Mechanical and energetic analyses revealed that pushing backward and sideways via knee extension is highly efficient. In contrast, pulling forward via knee flexion after heel strike easily slips on the floor, nearly doubling the Cost of Transport (CoT). Finally, the learned policy transferred zero-shot to a real Unitree G1, successfully demonstrating omnidirectional seated locomotion.
contributions: Demonstrated omnidirectional humanoid seated locomotion on a passive caster chair with unfixed pelvis-seat contact and direct foot propulsion, using reinforcement learning without reference motions.

Constructed an asymmetric actor-critic architecture where the actor relies solely on onboard proprioception and velocity commands—without chair states or contact sensors—achieving zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree G1.

Conducted a full-factorial analysis of symmetry regularization (SY), foot-slip regularization (FS), and command curriculum (CC), revealing that combining SY or CC with FS resolves the stationary local optimum caused by FS alone.

Clarified direction-dependent locomotion mechanics, showing that forward motion (knee flexion pull) slips more easily and incurs a significantly higher Cost of Transport (CoT) than backward or lateral motion (knee extension push).

sections.heading: Why put a humanoid robot on a chair to move around?
sections.summary: Standing during long desk work wastes energy and overheats QDD actuators, making sitting an attractive way to offload weight. As a first step toward seated loco-manipulation, this study investigates omnidirectional seated locomotion on a mobile chair with casters.
sections.details:
Recent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for humanoid locomotion mostly focuses on standing. However, the quasi-direct-drive (QDD) actuators common in modern robots must draw continuous current to support body weight even when standing still. This creates serious thermal and energy challenges.

Humans solve this during desk work by sitting down on office chairs. We offload our weight and scoot around with small foot pushes to adjust our position or view. If robots could perform similar seated loco-manipulation, they could handle extended tasks much more efficiently. As a first step, this paper investigates omnidirectional seated locomotion on a passive chair with casters.

The key challenge is that the robot's pelvis is not strapped to the chair. The robot must intermittently kick the floor to propel both itself and the chair. The authors investigate whether an agent can learn this coordinated behavior without human motion capture data, using only minimal extensions to an existing standing environment.

captions.F1: A real Unitree G1 translating and turning while seated on an office stool. The robot's body is not physically attached to the chair, autonomously balancing while generating propulsion.

sections.heading: How does this differ from wheeled tools, and why is it challenging?
sections.summary: While humanoid locomotion on skateboards or roller skates has been studied, feet are typically fixed or ground contact occurs purely through the tool. Seated locomotion introduces a novel contact topology with unfixed seat contact and direct foot propulsion.
sections.details:
Prior research on humanoid mobility with wheeled or sliding tools includes roller skates, skateboards, skis, and standing scooters. However, most of these setups fix the feet to the device or channel ground contact entirely through the tool. Skateboard setups do feature direct foot kicking, but riding and kicking occur in distinctly separate phases.

In contrast, seated locomotion requires two things at the same time: continuously maintaining unfixed pelvis-seat contact and kicking the floor directly to generate thrust. No prior reinforcement learning controller has solved this specific contact topology.

Furthermore, modern frameworks for natural humanoid motion rely heavily on reference motions, such as BeyondMimic or AMP. But capturing and retargeting synchronized human-and-chair motions across diverse directions and speeds is exceptionally difficult. This study therefore avoids reference motions entirely, learning the gait from scratch using only task rewards and regularizations.

sections.heading: Sit down and kick: simulation setup and training tricks
sections.summary: Building on a standing locomotion environment, the authors introduced a passive chair model, seated-state rewards, and an asymmetric actor-critic setup. Refining the pelvis collision mesh and friction settings proved essential, while SY, FS, and CC were evaluated to stabilize learning.
sections.details:
The simulation uses mjlab, featuring a 29-DoF Unitree G1 and a chair equipped with five casters (modeled as spheres on spherical joints) and a rotating seat. Key elements of the approach are detailed below.

- **III-A & B System Setup and Contact Modeling**
Velocity commands are specified in the torso frame: longitudinal and lateral speeds of $[-1.0, 1.0]$ m/s, and yaw rates of $[-0.5, 0.5]$ rad/s. Simulating the pelvis-seat contact was the most sensitive part. A coarse collision mesh or default pyramidal friction cone caused the pelvis to clip into the seat or slide off unnaturally. To fix this, the authors refined the pelvis collision mesh to match the visual geometry, adopted elliptic friction cones, and increased solver iterations to ensure stable contact dynamics.

- **III-C Asymmetric Actor-Critic Design**
To enable clean sim-to-real transfer, observations are split between actor and critic. The actor (96 dimensions) receives only real-world proprioception: joint positions, velocities, IMU readings, and velocity commands. It receives no chair states, seat contact states, or foot contact sensor values. The critic (217 dimensions) receives privileged information during training, including relative chair position and contact forces, allowing accurate value estimation.

- **III-D Reward Design and Three Learning Components**
Rewards include velocity tracking, posture maintenance, seated-state tracking (pelvis-chair distance and contact), and regularization penalties. The authors focused on three key learning strategies:
1. **SY (Symmetry Regularization)**: Applies bilateral reflection data augmentation and a mirror loss to the actor, promoting symmetric leg use.
2. **FS (Foot-Slip Penalty)**: Penalizes foot velocity during ground contact to improve energy efficiency.
3. **CC (Command Curriculum)**: Starts training at lower speeds ($[-0.5, 0.5]$ m/s) before expanding to higher speeds.

captions.F2: Overview of the seated locomotion learning framework. It highlights the asymmetric actor-critic structure (top-left), the refined pelvis collision mesh with the passive chair model (top-right), and the three evaluated training components (CC, SY, and FS, bottom).

sections.heading: Experimental results: Why does the foot-slip penalty alone freeze the robot?
sections.summary: Across eight conditions, policies combining SY and CC achieved the most consistent tracking, outperforming the standing policy. The foot-slip penalty (FS) alone caused policies to freeze under forward-diagonal commands, but combining FS with SY or CC fully resolved this failure.
sections.details:
Simulation evaluations included 20-second random command rollouts across 1,000 episodes and fixed-command grid sweeps to visualize tracking errors.

- **IV-A Overall Tracking Performance and Factorial Effects**
In random evaluations, over 99.45% of episodes across all conditions survived the full 20 seconds without falling or losing the chair. Policies trained with SY+CC and SY+FS+CC achieved lower root-mean-square tracking error (RMSE) than the standing policy.
However, the fixed-command heatmaps exposed a critical failure mode. When trained with FS alone, some seeds converged to a local optimum where the robot froze completely under forward-diagonal commands (Fig. F3(a)). The penalty on foot slipping was so strict that the policy simply gave up on pushing. Crucially, combining FS with either SY or CC eliminated this local optimum without needing to tune the FS penalty weight.

- **IV-B Direction-Resolved Gait Mechanics: Pushing Backward vs. Pulling Forward**
Measuring the Cost of Transport (CoT) across directions revealed striking differences. While differences were minor at 0.5 m/s, at 1.0 m/s the cost followed backward $<$ lateral $\ll$ forward. Forward CoT was nearly double that of lateral motion.
Kinematic analysis explained why. In backward and lateral motions, the robot plants its foot in front and pushes by extending the knee. In forward motion, the robot strikes the heel forward and pulls the body by flexing the knee. This pulling action easily exceeds friction limits and slips, meaning joint work does not translate efficiently into propulsion.

- **IV-C Zero-Shot Transfer to the Unitree G1**
The policy learned in simulation was deployed directly to a physical Unitree G1. Without any real-world fine-tuning, the robot smoothly translated forward, backward, sideways, and turned without slipping off the chair.

captions.F3: Tracking error heatmaps under fixed velocity commands. In (a) FS-only, a bad seed (left) shows dark red in forward-diagonal commands (top region), indicating a complete freeze. In contrast, (b) SY+FS, (c) FS+CC, and (d) SY+FS+CC successfully resolve this local optimum.
captions.F5: Simulation filmstrip showing a transition from rightward lateral motion to forward motion. Purple arrows represent command velocities and cyan arrows show measured velocities, illustrating smooth reorientation while seated.
captions.F6: Seated locomotion on the physical Unitree G1. Despite having no contact sensors or chair state feedback, the robot reproduces the foot coordination seen in simulation and glides smoothly.

sections.heading: Discussion: Differences from standing and open challenges
sections.summary: Because the chair supports body weight, seated locomotion permits asymmetric shortcuts like single-leg paddling, making symmetry regularization (SY) essential. Preliminary measurements also show sitting saves about 10 W at rest compared to standing.
sections.details:
Several interesting insights emerged from the findings.

First, why is symmetry natural in standing but fragile in seated locomotion? Standing robots must alternate both legs to support body weight and avoid falling, naturally leading to symmetric gaits. While seated, however, the chair supports body weight. A policy can easily satisfy velocity commands through asymmetric shortcuts, such as paddling with only one leg. Symmetry regularization (SY) is therefore vital to prevent one-sided hardware wear and ensure clean coordination.

Second, preliminary resting power measurements reported in the appendix yielded intriguing results. Standing still consumed an average of 111.06 W, whereas sitting still consumed 101.25 W—a reduction of roughly 9.81 W. On a 421.2 Wh battery, this translates to about 22 minutes of extra operating time. However, this was a preliminary single-trial measurement, and further verification is needed to generalize the energy savings of seated postures.

Future work includes exploring an "impulse-and-coast" strategy to take advantage of the high flight fraction (>60%) observed at 1.0 m/s forward motion, letting the chair coast on inertia after a strong kick. Applying this locomotion to seated loco-manipulation tasks between desks is another promising avenue.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.summary: The authors realized omnidirectional humanoid locomotion on a passive caster chair without motion imitation. The study showed how regularizations avoid local optima, uncovered directional gait mechanics, and validated zero-shot real-world transfer.
sections.details:
This work is the first to achieve omnidirectional humanoid seated locomotion on an unfixed passive mobile chair using reference-free deep reinforcement learning.

A factorial analysis demonstrated that while foot-slip penalties (FS) reduce the Cost of Transport, they can degrade tracking and trap policies in stationary local optima. Symmetry regularization (SY) and curricula (CC) serve as effective remedies. The work also uncovered fundamental mechanical differences between backward pushing and forward pulling gaits.

Seeing the real Unitree G1 scoot smoothly without chair tracking or contact sensors opens up an exciting new form of mobility for humanoids in everyday environments.

takeaways: When body weight is externally supported, robots can easily adopt asymmetric shortcuts; symmetry regularization (SY) is crucial for eliciting clean bilateral coordination.
Penalties like foot-slip regularization can induce freezing local optima when used alone; combining them with curriculum learning (CC) or data augmentation (SY) avoids this failure.
Just like humans on office chairs, humanoids find pulling forward with heel contact far more prone to slipping and energetically inefficient than pushing backward with knee extension.

Complex tool-based whole-body locomotion can transfer zero-shot to real hardware without contact sensors or external tracking, provided collision meshes and asymmetric actor-critic setups are carefully tuned.
limitations: Real-world evaluations were qualitative demonstrations; quantitative assessments of velocity tracking accuracy and disturbance robustness on hardware were not conducted.
Resting power consumption was measured in only a single preliminary trial, without isolating individual actuator power draw or thermal characteristics.
Experiments were limited to a single chair model, one floor friction condition, and a specific command velocity range.
